text: {"title":"Understanding filter() returns a QuerySet","body":"First, name the mistaken idea: many students hear Post.objects.filter(...) and assume the call gives the single matching post, so they try to read a field directly from the result. That intuition feels right because in many examples the filter happens to match exactly one row, and the error they see mentions a QuerySet rather than the field they expected.\\nNext, expose the break: ask them to run a filter that is guaranteed to return more than one object, such as Post.objects.filter(id__in=[1,3]) from the material. When they then try to access .title on that result they get an AttributeError about the QuerySet, showing that the operation does not return a single model instance. This single counter‑example shatters the “single record” model.\\nNow give the correct model: filter always produces another QuerySet, a collection that may contain zero, one, or many objects. To obtain a single object you must use get() when you know exactly one matches, or use .first(), .last() or indexing after confirming the size with .count() or .exists() as described in the text.\\nFinally, tell them what to watch for: after any filter, treat the result as iterable; before accessing a field, either iterate, pick an element, or explicitly call get()/first(). If they ever see a QuerySet in an error message, that is the cue to remember that filter never returns a bare model instance."}
